claims.text: Fucha ryori is defined by its skillful use of oil and includes deep-fried dishes (tempura, fried imitation items); these batters are typically wheat-based, so gluten cross-contact in fryers is likely. Not confirmed whether any GF accommodation exists.

As a traditional Japanese temple kitchen, the cuisine uses standard soy sauce and sweet glazes, which normally contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is advertised. Assume soy seasonings contain gluten unless confirmed.
This is a Buddhist (shojin/fucha) kitchen serving no meat, fish or animal products, so animal cross-contact is inherently minimal — a strong positive for vegans and vegetarians.

Meals are completely reservation-only and arranged 2-3 days in advance, which gives the kitchen the opportunity to note dietary needs; however, no published allergen protocol was found, so specific allergies should be raised directly when booking.
Entirely plant-based Buddhist temple cuisine — no meat or fish in the kitchen — making it one of the safest choices in Kyoto for vegans and vegetarians.
Shojin/fucha tradition uses kombu and shiitake dashi rather than fish-based dashi, so the umami base is plant-derived.

name: 豆乳ラーメン専門店 豆禅 (MameZen (Tonyu Ramen Senmonten Towzen))

claims.text: Kitchen uses a single boiling pot, but separate preparation is available on request, important for a celiac ordering gluten-free rice noodles alongside wheat ramen.
A wheat-free soy sauce is used when the gluten-free rice noodles are selected; standard ramen uses wheat noodles.
Kitchen is 100% vegan with no animal products on premises, so there is no meat, fish or dairy cross-contact.
Menu explicitly offers gluten-free rice noodles and notes separate preparation can be requested.
Fully vegan, animal-free kitchen rooted in shojin cuisine, no fish dashi, eggs or dairy anywhere, very low-risk for vegan travelers.
Offers a genuine gluten-free path (rice noodles plus wheat-free soy sauce), uncommon for a ramen shop.

name: オーシーブリトー（旧店名：ラ セグンダ ホヤ SUINA室町店） (OC Burrito (formerly La Segunda Jolla, S)

claims.text: Casual shared-line counter where flour (wheat) tortillas are handled alongside corn tortillas; no dedicated gluten-free protocol is documented, so cross-contact with wheat is possible. Request corn tortillas and ask staff.

Vegan and vegetarian items are prepared on the same counter line as meat, cheese and dairy lime cream; the explicitly Vegan Taco BOX and Vegan Burrito are designed to be plant-based, but shared utensils/surfaces mean some animal cross-contact is possible at a busy counter.
Staff have accommodated plant-based requests off-menu, including cooking rice separately without chicken stock for a vegan guest, indicating willingness to adjust on request.
Offers clearly labeled vegan items (Vegan Taco BOX on corn tortillas with green rice, black beans, salsa and chips; Vegan Burrito), so plant-based diners do not have to fully improvise.
Emphasizes fresh vegetables prepared daily and made-fresh guacamole and salsa.

name: ペッティロッソ 京都 (Pettirosso Kyoto)

claims.text: The kitchen is entirely plant-based with no animal products used, which greatly reduces the risk of meat, fish or dairy cross-contact.
Listings recommend telling the staff about your vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies when choosing from the menu, and the owners speak good English so this is easy to do.
Fully vegan kitchen since May 2023 - no animal products at all, so no meat/fish/dairy in the kitchen.
Owners speak very good English and the vegan menu is well marked, making it easy to ask about ingredients.
Gluten-free sweets are offered and a reviewer noted plenty of gluten-free options alongside the vegan ones.
Freshly baked chapati (wheat) is part of the standard set and fried snacks use batter, so wheat is handled openly in the kitchen; no gluten-free accommodation is indicated.
This is an omnivore kitchen that also cooks fish/meat curries and dairy items (lassi, yogurt, paneer) in the same small space, so vegan dishes are prepared alongside animal products.

Vegetarian options are explicitly available, but the owner runs a fast, no-reservations counter with strict house rules and limited time per customer, so make any vegan/allergy requests quickly and clearly.

Vegetarian options are confirmed available, and the daily plate already includes multiple plant-based vegetable and legume curries (e.g. potato-tomato and chana/chickpea), giving a vegetarian or flexible-vegan diner real choices.
Curries are described as light, home-style and gentle on the body rather than heavy, with an inexpensive all-in set plate.

name: プレマルシェ・ジェラテリア 三条本店 (Premarché Gelateria Kyoto Sanjo (Honten))

claims.text: The shop states none of its gelato contains gluten-containing ingredients; main residual concern is the serving vessel (standard cones/waffle cups), so request the rice-based gluten-free option.
Vegan and dairy gelato are scooped from the same case, so shared scoops/utensils mean some dairy cross-contact is possible; fine for dietary vegans but worth asking if you have a milk allergy.
Allergy information is available and the shop explicitly accommodates food allergies on request, with alternative serving vessels for wheat-allergic guests.
All gelato is gluten-free and a dedicated gluten-free organic mochi waffle cup (~¥100) is offered for wheat-allergic guests.
One of Japan's largest selections of vegan and non-dairy gelato, with clearly distinguished pure-vegan and sorbetto options made from fruit and sugar only.
Award-winning vegan gelato (3rd place in an international Italian Gelato Association contest) signals genuine expertise in plant-based recipes.

This is a wheat-heavy burrito kitchen (flour tortillas); no gluten-free preparation or cross-contamination control is documented, so celiac diners should treat it as unsafe unless they confirm details directly.
It is an omnivore kitchen serving beef and pork alongside vegan items, so shared surfaces and utensils are likely; ask for clean preparation if strict.
Owner is described as English-speaking, knowledgeable about veganism, and accommodating, willing to omit cheese/sour cream and build custom vegan burritos (e.g., tofu, shiitake) on request.
Vegan diners can get a substantial, flavorful burrito or taco with three fresh salsas, and the staff actively understands and supports vegan requests.
A dedicated all-vegan menu is offered roughly once a month for fully animal-free dining.

name: 素食カフェRen 堀川商店街店 (Soshoku Cafe Ren (Horikawa Shotengai bra)

claims.text: No gluten-free information is published. The menu centers on wheat-based dumplings, gyoza, radish cakes, glutinous-rice dumplings and noodles, and Taiwanese mock meats commonly contain wheat gluten, so wheat cross-contact is likely. Gluten-sensitive diners should ask about each dish.
Whether the soy sauce is wheat-free is not stated anywhere; assume standard wheat-containing soy sauce until confirmed in person.
The entire kitchen is fully plant-based with no meat, fish, eggs or dairy used at all, so there is no animal-product cross-contact — a strong positive for vegan diners.
Guests are advised to inform staff of dietary restrictions and allergies before ordering; the owner/staff are reported as friendly and English-speaking, which helps with allergy questions.
100% vegan kitchen — no meat, fish, eggs or dairy anywhere on the menu, eliminating animal cross-contact entirely.
Allium-free cooking: no onion, garlic, scallion or chives are used (Buddhist 'five pungent vegetables' avoided), helpful for those sensitive to alliums.
Friendly, English-speaking owner/staff who serve a complimentary herbal soup, making it easy to discuss what's in each dish.
